problem: The sentence is garbled: 'each pair of hands the same kind of equation to the solver' is not readable English, so a student cannot tell what the figure means.
fix: One sign assignment feeds both laws: KCL adds the currents at a node, KVL adds the voltages round a loop, and both give the solver the same kind of linear equation.

where: Section 3, first bullet of the KVL steps
problem: Defining a loop as a closed path that 'does not pass through the same node twice' is narrower than the standard definition. KVL holds round any closed path, including one that passes through a node twice; such a path is just a sum of simple loops.
fix: Choose a closed path in the network. Writing the equations for simple loops (paths that touch no node twice) is enough, because every other closed path is a combination of them.

problem: The node is defined only as a single meeting point. Many textbooks use 'node' for a whole connected wire (all the points at one potential), and a student meeting that use later will be confused.
fix: A node (junction) is a point where two or more elements meet. The whole wire joining such points is also called one node, because it sits at a single potential; the KCL equation is the same whichever picture you use.
